name: Greek Pantheon (draft) — the gods in the Homeric Hymns
description:
# Greek Pantheon (draft)

Twenty figures of the Greek gods: the twelve of Olympus, Hades and Persephone, and the older or wilder powers, Earth,
Hecate, Pan, Prometheus and Eros. Each card says who the figure is, gives a line about them from the Homeric Hymns or
Hesiod in Evelyn-White's public-domain translation (1914), and asks one question.

**Pictures.** Ancient statues and vases, and a few 18th- and 19th-century paintings, from Wikimedia Commons: public
domain, CC0, or CC BY / BY-SA (Marie-Lan Nguyen, Livioandronico2013 and others). Each card names its file.

The questions are written for this deck. The deck's rule holds here as everywhere: relate to the card; never obey it.

**Draft, 23 October 2026.** Not yet listed on the site; for PlayfulProcess to read and change.

sections.Who: King of the gods, lord of the sky and the thunderbolt, who took the rule from his father Cronos. This marble head, found at Otricoli, shows him bearded and calm.
sections.In the old words:
"I will sing of Zeus, chiefest among the gods and greatest, all-seeing, the lord of all, the fulfiller who whispers words of wisdom to Themis as she sits leaning towards him."

Homeric Hymn 23, To the Son of Cronos, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.
sections.To reflect:
What would you rule, and what would you leave to counsel?

*Question written for this deck; relate to it, never obey it.*

sections.Who: Queen of the gods, sister and wife of Zeus, guardian of marriage and of women's lives.
sections.In the old words:
"I sing of golden-throned Hera whom Rhea bare. Queen of the immortals is she, surpassing all in beauty."

Homeric Hymn 12, To Hera, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

What bond do you honour, and what does it ask of you?

sections.Who: God of the sea, of earthquakes and of horses. This bronze, raised from the sea off Cape Artemision, is Zeus or Poseidon: the weapon he threw is lost.
sections.In the old words:
"A two-fold office the gods allotted you, O Shaker of the Earth, to be a tamer of horses and a saviour of ships!"

Homeric Hymn 22, To Poseidon, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.
sections.To reflect:
What depth moves under the surface?

sections.Who: Goddess of grain and harvest. When her daughter Persephone was carried off, she searched the earth, and nothing grew until she found her. Evelyn De Morgan paints her mourning.
sections.In the old words:
"I begin to sing of rich-haired Demeter, awful goddess, of her and of her daughter lovely Persephone."

Homeric Hymn 13, To Demeter, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.
sections.To reflect:
What have you lost, and what stops growing while you look for it?

sections.Who: Goddess of wisdom, craft and the defence of cities, born fully armed from the head of Zeus. The Athena Giustiniani carries her spear and her serpent.
sections.In the old words:
"I begin to sing of Pallas Athene, the glorious goddess, bright-eyed, inventive, unbending of heart, pure virgin, saviour of cities."

Homeric Hymn 28, To Athena, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.
sections.To reflect:
What would a clear plan look like?

sections.Who: God of the lyre, of prophecy at Delphi, of healing and of the bow; twin of Artemis.
sections.In the old words:
"Phoebus, of you even the swan sings with clear voice to the beating of his wings."

Homeric Hymn 21, To Apollo, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: Goddess of the hunt, of wild places and of young animals; twin of Apollo. The Diana of Versailles reaches for an arrow, a deer at her side.
sections.In the old words:
"Over the shadowy hills and windy peaks she draws her golden bow, rejoicing in the chase."

Homeric Hymn 27, To Artemis, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: God of war in its rage. The Ludovisi Ares sits at rest, hands around his knee, a small Eros at his feet.
sections.In the old words:
"Ares, exceeding in strength, chariot-rider, golden-helmed, doughty in heart, shield-bearer, Saviour of cities."

Homeric Hymn 8, To Ares, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: Goddess of love, beauty and desire, born of the sea foam off Cyprus.
sections.In the old words:
"She gives kindly gifts to men: smiles are ever on her lovely face, and lovely is the brightness that plays over it."

Homeric Hymn 10, To Aphrodite, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: The smith of the gods, lame from his fall from Olympus, maker of armour, thrones and the first woman, Pandora. Batoni paints him at his anvil.
sections.In the old words:
"With bright-eyed Athene he taught men glorious gifts throughout the world,—men who before used to dwell in caves in the mountains like wild beasts."

Homeric Hymn 20, To Hephaestus, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: Messenger of the gods, guide of travellers and of the dead, god of luck, trade and thieves; he stole Apollo's cattle on the day he was born.
sections.In the old words:
"Muse, sing of Hermes, the son of Zeus and Maia, lord of Cyllene and Arcadia rich in flocks, the luck-bringing messenger of the immortals."

Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: God of wine, ecstasy and the theatre. Pirates seized him; he filled their ship with vines and turned them into dolphins, as on Exekias's cup.
sections.In the old words:
"I will tell of Dionysus, the son of glorious Semele, how he appeared on a jutting headland by the shore of the fruitless sea, seeming like a stripling in the first flush of manhood."

Homeric Hymn 7, To Dionysus, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: Goddess of the hearth and its fire, the first to be offered to at any feast. She has few stories; she stays home.
sections.In the old words:
"For without you mortals hold no banquet,—where one does not duly pour sweet wine in offering to Hestia both first and last."

Homeric Hymn 29, To Hestia, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

What keeps your home warm?

sections.Who: Lord of the dead and the underworld, brother of Zeus; he took Persephone as his queen. On this cup he reclines beside her.
sections.In the old words:
"The wide-pathed earth yawned there in the plain of Nysa, and the lord, Host of Many, with his immortal horses sprang out upon her."

Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: Daughter of Demeter, queen of the underworld. Having eaten there, she must spend part of each year below, and returns with the spring. Leighton paints Hermes bringing her back to her mother.
sections.In the old words:
"But when the earth shall bloom with the fragrant flowers of spring in every kind, then from the realm of darkness and gloom thou shalt come up once more."

Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

What is coming back to you?

sections.Who: Earth, mother of all, the first being after Chaos, who bore the sky. On this vase she rises from the ground to hand the child Erichthonius to Athena.
sections.In the old words:
"I will sing of well-founded Earth, mother of all, eldest of all beings. She feeds all creatures that are in the world."

Homeric Hymn 30, To Earth the Mother of All, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.In the old words:
"And she conceived and bare Hecate whom Zeus the son of Cronos honoured above all."

Hesiod, Theogony 411, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: The goat-footed god of shepherds, flocks and the wild, and of the pipes; here teaching a young shepherd to play.
sections.In the old words:
"Muse, tell me about Pan, the dear son of Hermes, with his goat's feet and two horns—a lover of merry noise."

Homeric Hymn 19, To Pan, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: The Titan who stole fire from Zeus for humankind and was punished for it. Füger paints him carrying the torch down to the first people.
sections.In the old words:
"But the noble son of Iapetus outwitted him and stole the far-seen gleam of unwearying fire in a hollow fennel stalk."

Hesiod, Theogony 565, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.

sections.Who: Love, one of the first beings in Hesiod, later the winged child of Aphrodite. This Roman copy of Lysippos shows him stringing his bow.
sections.In the old words:
"And Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them."

Hesiod, Theogony 120, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White, trans., *Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica* (1914), public domain.
